paragraphs: This paper develops a neural architecture in which several networks share a task by learning different parts of it. The motivation is that useful task structure can lie between highly local relationships and a single global relationship. A collection of specialized networks offers a way to represent this intermediate level of organization.

The central mechanism combines associative learning with competition. The component networks compete to learn training examples, and different networks consequently become responsible for different patterns. This process partitions the input space through training. The division of work is therefore something the architecture discovers, rather than a task decomposition that must be fully specified beforehand.

The paper presents performance on a vision task involving object identity and location, and on a robotics task involving multiple payloads. These applications illustrate the intended role of learned specialization across different settings. The contribution is an architecture that makes discovering the task's internal organization part of learning how to perform it.
neurips-1990-a-competitive-modular-conne.tldr: Competing neural modules learn to divide a task into specialized parts by taking responsibility for different training examples.

paragraphs: This paper models the initial turn a cockroach makes when escaping a puff of wind. The biological circuit contains three populations of individually identifiable nerve cells and appears to represent information across multiple cells. The study asks how this distributed activity can account for both neuronal responses and the animal's turning behavior.

The researchers build simplified neural networks and train them with backpropagation, while restricting their structure according to known features of the biological circuitry. Those constraints connect the learning problem to the actual nervous system. The resulting models reconstruct several properties of the neurons and behavior, showing how a simplified circuit can capture aspects of the transformation from sensory input to movement.

The researchers also compare the effects of lesions in the model with responses to similar lesions in the insect. These comparisons serve to test and refine the model beyond its ordinary responses. The approach matters because matching behavior after circuit damage provides another way to assess a proposed explanation of distributed sensorimotor control.
neurips-1990-a-model-of-distributed-sens.tldr: An anatomically constrained neural model reconstructs aspects of the cockroach escape turn and is tested against biological lesion responses.

paragraphs: This paper describes a working electronic system for color constancy: keeping perceived object colors relatively stable when illumination changes. Its computational basis is Land's Retinex theory. In the supplied account, that theory applies the same center-surround operation independently to three color channels, relating color processing to the spatial surroundings of an image location.

The researchers implement the system using three custom chips built with subthreshold analog CMOS technology. Resistive grids on the chips perform the smoothing operation that the algorithm requires. This physical implementation carries out that operation at video rates, making spatial color correction something the hardware can perform on a moving stream of images.

The system was built and successfully tested, producing colors that resemble those of human vision in several respects. The electronic implementation also provides a way to investigate the algorithm's strengths and weaknesses. The contribution therefore joins a perceptual theory with functioning hardware, allowing the proposed computation to be examined through the behavior of an actual color-correction system.
neurips-1990-a-vlsi-neural-network-for-c.tldr: Three custom analog chips implement Retinex color correction, using resistive grids to perform spatial smoothing at video rates.

paragraphs: This paper turns a theory of psychological generalization into a connectionist model. The starting observation is that learning transfers less strongly as a test stimulus becomes more distant from a training stimulus in a space representing perceived similarity. Empirically, this decline closely follows an exponential relationship, giving the theory a specific pattern to explain.

The theory assumes that an observed consequential stimulus belongs to a broader consequential region. The learner knows that the observed stimulus lies inside this region, but initially does not know the region's position, size, or shape. Uncertainty about that region supplies a mathematical basis for predicting how strongly learning should extend to other stimuli.

Additional examples indicate which stimuli do or do not have the consequence. The theory predicts that generalization then changes toward the actual relationship between stimulus location and consequence probability. The paper implements this account in a neural model and uses simulations to explore its implications for generalization, discrimination, and classification. This makes an abstract account of similarity-based learning available for computational investigation.
neurips-1990-connectionist-implementatio.tldr: A connectionist implementation explores how uncertainty about consequential stimulus regions shapes generalization and changes with experience.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether the vectors adjusted by the LVQ classification algorithm settle down as learning proceeds. Convergence matters because repeated updates alone do not establish that a learning process approaches a stable result. The authors provide a proof of vector convergence by connecting the algorithm to a mathematical framework for learning from noisy observations.

That framework is stochastic approximation. Viewing LVQ through it allows the authors to identify conditions involving the learning rate and the statistical properties of the classification problem. The guarantee is therefore conditional: stability follows when the update schedule and the underlying data statistics satisfy the appropriate requirements.

The paper also proposes a modification aimed at a stronger objective than stable vectors. The authors argue that its classification error approaches the Bayesian optimal error as suitable parameters become large. This is the best error achievable given the classification problem's underlying probabilities. The distinction matters: the first result establishes convergence of the representation, while the second addresses how accurate the resulting classifier can ultimately become.
neurips-1990-convergence-of-a-neural-net.tldr: The paper proves conditional convergence of LVQ vectors and argues that a modified algorithm can approach Bayesian optimal classification error.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how organized feature maps can develop in the visual cortex. Cells selective for visual position, orientation, and ocular dominance form spatial patterns rather than an arbitrary arrangement. The researchers use a self-organizing neural network to study how such organization can arise and why the resulting maps have their observed spatial structure.

The model treats map formation as a reduction from a high-dimensional feature space to a two-dimensional lattice. Each feature combination has a location in the richer space, while cells occupy positions on the lattice. The organizing principle translates similarity between features into physical proximity between the cells that represent them.

The network reproduces several aspects of cortical map structure. This supports the usefulness of dimension reduction and similarity preservation as modeling principles for these arrangements. The result links development and spatial organization within one computational account: the process that builds the map also explains aspects of which feature-selective cells become neighbors. Its stated success concerns several structural features of cortical maps.
neurips-1990-development-and-spatial-str.tldr: A self-organizing model reproduces aspects of cortical feature maps by placing similar feature representations near one another on a two-dimensional lattice.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical connection between wavelet transforms and feedforward neural networks. Wavelets describe functions through components localized in both position and frequency. The authors show that wavelet frames for square-integrable functions of one real variable can be constructed from sigmoid functions, linking this representation to the building blocks of standard neural networks.

That connection supplies a method for both analyzing networks and constructing them. The localization properties of wavelets guide the choice of network topology and weights. Architecture design therefore becomes tied to the structure of a function representation, giving a principled route from the function being modeled to the network used to represent it.

For networks built with the proposed synthesis procedure, training minimizes a convex cost functional. The authors present this as a way to avoid pitfalls associated with standard backpropagation. The convexity claim applies to their construction, making the choice of representation central to the optimization benefit. The paper also discusses extending the method from functions of one variable to functions of multiple variables.
neurips-1990-discrete-affine-wavelet-tra.tldr: Sigmoid-based wavelet representations guide feedforward network construction and yield a convex training objective for the proposed synthesis procedure.

paragraphs: This paper studies how specific connections between the eye and brain develop and regenerate. Both processes involve forming an organized map between neural populations. The researchers use a computational model to investigate how such organization can emerge, considering both the initial construction of the circuitry and its reconstruction during regeneration.

The model combines a self-organizing network with local Hebbian learning rules and genetically determined molecular markers. The local rules provide a mechanism for adapting connections through activity, while the markers constrain that adaptation. Map formation thus depends on an interaction between learning within the network and biological guidance encoded in its molecular organization.

The paper describes simulations of development and regeneration in fish and frogs, including successful simulations of several named experimental studies. These results show that the proposed combination can reproduce outcomes across the biological situations examined. The approach matters because it brings developmental guidance and local adaptation into one model, allowing the same computational ingredients to be studied in both map formation and regeneration.
neurips-1990-further-studies-of-a-model-.tldr: A self-organizing model combines local Hebbian learning with molecular guidance to simulate eye-brain map development and regeneration.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether the TLS theory of learning can predict how models learn probability densities from examples. In this setting, the learner receives samples and adjusts a model of fixed form to approximate the distribution that generated them. The aim is to understand average training behavior through a general theory.

The authors first analyze an elementary problem, finding that the theory agrees with conventional statistical results. They then conduct a numerical study of a competitive network learning a probability density. These two applications connect an analytically accessible case with a more realistic neural learning problem, testing the theory in complementary ways.

The supplied account also explains that TLS can be derived through maximum entropy, rather than depending essentially on its original statistical-mechanics formulation. Its construction requires independent examples and an additive function whose average is specified. Under this framework, the authors find the theory useful for predicting average training behavior. The contribution is therefore both an interpretation of the theory and evidence of its usefulness for density learning.
neurips-1990-learning-theory-and-experim.tldr: Analytical and numerical studies find TLS theory useful for predicting average behavior when learning probability densities from samples.

paragraphs: This paper asks what an array of visual filters should look like if it is designed to preserve information from natural images. The filters are linear, and their information capacity is optimized under two constraints: noise in individual channels and a cost for building connections over long distances. These constraints make the design problem sensitive to both signal quality and wiring.

At low signal-to-noise ratios, the optimal filters can be described using bound states of a Schrödinger equation. In this mathematical correspondence, the image signal's spectrum plays the role of the potential. The equation supplies a way to derive filter shapes from image statistics and the constraints imposed on the array.

The resulting filters closely resemble ones observed in mammalian visual cortex and in retinal ganglion cells of lower vertebrates. The scale invariance of natural images is essential to the construction. The finding suggests that these biological filter shapes can be understood through constrained information optimization, with their structure linked to regularities in the visual environment.
neurips-1990-optimal-sampling-of-natural.tldr: Optimizing image information under noise and wiring costs produces filters resembling biological visual filters in the low-signal regime.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to update a radial basis function network as observations arrive one after another. The network uses Gaussian nodes, and the adaptation method is based on successive F-Projections. The focus is on extracting useful information from each observation while updating the function represented by the network.

The proposed procedure produces a mapping consistent with the information in an observation and optimal according to a least L2-norm criterion. That criterion gives the update a defined mathematical objective. Rather than treating efficient use of data only as an empirical goal, the method builds a particular notion of consistency and optimality into the adaptation procedure.

The researchers apply the network to prediction of a chaotic time series and compare it with an adaptation method based on stochastic approximation. They report much faster convergence toward the underlying model with F-Projections. The stated result concerns the rate at which the learned mapping approaches that model, showing the practical importance of the adaptation rule alongside the choice of network representation.
neurips-1990-sequential-adaptation-of-ra.tldr: Successive F-Projections adapt Gaussian RBF networks sequentially and converge faster than stochastic approximation in the reported chaotic time-series task.

paragraphs: This paper extends a speech recognizer based on pattern prediction by multilayer perceptrons. The earlier model had shown effectiveness in speaker-independent digit recognition. The new work improves its prediction mechanism and applies it to a larger vocabulary, using units smaller than whole words as the basis for recognition.

The model adds backward prediction to its existing forward prediction. This gives the prediction process an additional direction, and the authors report that it improves prediction accuracy. For the large-vocabulary application, the system uses demi-syllables as subword units. This choice provides intermediate speech components through which the recognizer can handle the word vocabulary.

The large-vocabulary experiment is speaker-dependent and reports 95.2% recognition accuracy on a 5,000-word test set. The results support both the added backward prediction and the use of demi-syllable units. The distinction between the earlier and current settings matters: the speaker-independent evidence concerns digits, while the stated large-vocabulary result concerns recognition adapted to a speaker.
neurips-1990-speech-recognition-using-de.tldr: Backward prediction and demi-syllable units improve a neural speech model that achieves 95.2% accuracy on a speaker-dependent 5,000-word test set.

paragraphs: This paper addresses stereo correspondence: deciding which pixels in two views refer to the same scene content. It considers possible matches along corresponding epipolar lines and expresses the decision as a nonlinear, many-to-one mapping. The goal is to learn that mapping so that recognition of the correct correspondence can proceed without an iterative matching process.

The authors train a two-layer feedforward network with backpropagation. Constraints such as uniqueness and continuity are not explicitly inserted into the system. Instead, the network learns the applicable restrictions from examples and encodes them internally. This shifts a central part of stereo matching from specifying rules by hand to learning how valid matches behave.

Tests on several random-dot stereograms are reported as successful, including generalization to examples outside the training set. The paper also reports superior performance relative to the Marr-Poggio algorithm. These findings support the approach in the examined setting: a learned mapping can capture useful correspondence constraints and apply them beyond the specific stereo patterns used during training.
neurips-1990-stereopsis-by-a-neural-netw.tldr: A feedforward stereo network learns matching constraints from examples and generalizes successfully to unseen random-dot stereograms.

paragraphs: This paper examines two commonly repeated claims about neural networks: that they remain effective after component damage, and that dense connectivity is necessary for efficient use of resources. The authors turn these broad intuitions into questions for formal analysis. Their organizing device is a hypothetical agent that removes connections, progressively making the network sparse.

Connection removal provides a way to investigate how computational ability depends on the network's wiring. The two claims concern different aspects of that dependence. Robustness asks whether computation survives damage, while resource efficiency asks whether extensive interconnection is necessary to make good use of the available neural elements.

The supplied text explicitly rejects an unrestricted robustness claim. A network that depends on a critical, highly specialized cell can lose its computational ability when that cell is damaged. This example shows why the arrangement of a computation matters alongside its overall connectivity. The paper's stated contribution is to formally examine these assumptions about sparsity, damage, and resource use, rather than treating robustness as an automatic property of neural computation.
neurips-1990-the-devil-and-the-network-w.tldr: The paper formally examines whether neural networks tolerate connection loss and whether efficient computation requires dense connectivity.

paragraphs: Recurrent Cascade-Correlation is an architecture for learning a desired output sequence from an input sequence. It extends Cascade-Correlation by adding hidden units with recurrent connections during training. These connections support sequence-dependent computation, while the growing architecture lets the network develop the internal structure needed for the particular problem.

The supplied description explains the underlying construction process. Training begins with connections between inputs and outputs. When progress stalls and error remains too high, candidate hidden units are trained to correlate with the remaining error. The best candidate is added to the active network, with its incoming weights frozen. This makes network growth responsive to what the current model still fails to capture.

In the recurrent version, the authors describe the resulting system as effectively building a task-specific finite-state machine. They report retaining fast learning, good generalization, incremental training, and automatic construction of a near-minimal multilayer network. The approach matters because learning determines both the sequence mapping and much of the machinery used to represent it.
neurips-1990-the-recurrent-cascade-corre.tldr: Recurrent Cascade-Correlation grows recurrent hidden units during training to construct a compact network tailored to a sequence-learning problem.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a method for learning the timing of information used by a neural network. Alongside connection weights, the method adjusts time delays and the widths of temporal windows. These parameters determine when a unit draws on input information and how broad an interval of that information contributes to its computation.

The mechanism uses a Gaussian window to weight inputs over time. This formulation lets learning rules for the delays and window widths be derived in the same manner as rules for the connection weights. Temporal selection becomes part of supervised learning, allowing training to adjust both the influence of an input and its timing.

The authors evaluate the method on phoneme classification and report results that compare well with a time-delay neural network manually optimized for the same task. The significance is that useful temporal settings can be learned automatically within the network. The comparison supports automatic adjustment as an effective way to configure the temporal processing required for the reported speech task.
neurips-1990-the-tempo-2-algorithm-adjus.tldr: Tempo 2 learns time delays and temporal window widths automatically, with phoneme-classification results comparable to a manually optimized TDNN.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way to simplify neural networks during training so that they generalize better. It adds a complexity penalty to the ordinary error function. The defining idea is that a set of weights is simple when its values can be organized into groups whose members are similar.

The penalty models the distribution of weights as a mixture of Gaussian distributions. Each component supports a cluster of nearby weight values, encouraging a form of soft sharing across the network. The mixture parameters adapt while the network learns, so the preferred groups are themselves learned rather than fully fixed before training begins.

Simulations find this complexity term more effective than the previous terms considered. The result supports similarity among weights as a useful form of network simplicity. It also highlights the role of adaptation in the penalty: the learning process can discover which collections of weights should have related values while continuing to fit the task. Generalization is addressed through the organization of the parameters themselves.
neurips-1991-adaptive-soft-weight-tying-.tldr: An adaptive Gaussian-mixture penalty encourages clusters of similar network weights and outperforms earlier complexity penalties in the reported simulations.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether neural networks can locate a particular wave in graphical results from a medical test. The input is ordered in time, and the task is to identify the target wave's location. This focuses the recognition problem on a feature within a trace, rather than on assigning a label to the entire test.

The researchers perform five experiments using several network architectures. The first establishes a baseline of correct target identification in 85% of 20 cases. Other experiments examine how the network architecture and preprocessing of the raw data affect the results, treating both representation and model design as parts of the recognition problem.

The authors conclude that the methods appear best suited to time-oriented graphs with a clear starting point, such as electrophoresis or spectrometry. They distinguish these from continuous recordings such as ECGs and EEGs. This stated scope matters because a defined beginning gives the graphical sequence a shared temporal reference. The findings therefore support a particular kind of wave-location application rather than unrestricted analysis of medical traces.
neurips-1991-computer-recognition-of-wav.tldr: Five experiments explore neural wave localization in medical graphs, with an initial 85% success rate and strongest suitability for traces with clear starting points.

paragraphs: This paper describes a system that recognizes names spelled aloud over the telephone. Speakers leave brief pauses between letters, giving the recognizer a sequence of spoken letter names to process. The task combines identifying individual letters with deciding which complete name best matches the available speech evidence.

Separate neural networks locate segment boundaries and classify the letters within those segments. The resulting letter scores are then used to search a database of names. This preserves the role of letter-level evidence while using the name collection to make the final decision. Recognition therefore spans both the acoustic pieces and the complete item being requested.

The system achieves an 89% speaker-independent classification rate for spoken letters. It retrieves the correct name 91% of the time from a database containing 50,000 names when names are spelled with pauses. These are distinct measures: one assesses individual letters, while the other assesses the final database result. Together, they demonstrate the reported performance of the component recognizer and the complete name-retrieval system.
neurips-1991-english-alphabet-recognitio.tldr: Neural letter recognition and database scoring retrieve telephone-spelled names with 91% accuracy from a collection of 50,000 names.

paragraphs: This paper extends the time-delay neural network into a Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network for word recognition. A central issue is how to manage the sequence of smaller speech units that makes up a word. Recognizing those components must be coordinated with their order and their alignment to the incoming speech.

The architecture embeds an alignment search inside the neural system and allows supervision at the word level. This connects the handling of subword sequences directly to the recognition objective. Training can therefore operate on the desired word outcome while the architecture manages the internal alignment needed to relate that outcome to the speech signal.

The paper presents extensive evaluations on connected alphabet speech in both speaker-dependent and speaker-independent settings. These settings examine the approach with different relationships between training speakers and recognition use. The central contribution is the integration of alignment and neural recognition within one architecture, making sequential organization part of the system being optimized for recognizer performance.
neurips-1991-multi-state-time-delay-netw.tldr: The MS-TDNN embeds alignment search within a neural speech recognizer, enabling word-level supervision while managing subword order.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how multilayer neural networks can be combined with probability-density models, especially Gaussian mixtures used in continuous-density hidden Markov models. The aim is to connect neural computation with a probabilistic representation useful for speech recognition. It also examines what such a connection means for estimating distributions more generally.

The first part presents a neural-network and hidden-Markov-model hybrid whose parameters are all optimized simultaneously using one criterion. This gives the combined system a shared training objective. The contribution is therefore not only placing two model types together, but arranging learning so that their adjustable parts are optimized as components of the same system.

The second part studies the relationship between the probability density of network inputs and the density of its outputs. That relationship matters when interpreting a network's transformation as part of density estimation. A few experiments explore how neural networks can perform this task. Together, the two parts investigate both joint training for a speech-oriented hybrid and the distributional questions underlying neural density modeling.
neurips-1991-neural-network-gaussian-mix.tldr: The paper jointly trains a neural-network/HMM hybrid and explores how network transformations can support probability-density estimation.

paragraphs: This paper proposes growing a network by splitting hidden nodes after a smaller network has learned an approximate solution. The larger network inherits that solution, giving further learning an informed starting point. The method looks for places where the current model needs more detail, using oscillation in hidden-node weight vectors as evidence of insufficient capacity.

Principal component analysis identifies oscillating nodes and supports splitting each into two nodes covering the main modes of its changing weight vector. The paper also considers selecting nodes through the Hessian, which describes second derivatives of the error with respect to weights. Applied at the input layer, this second-derivative analysis can indicate the relative importance of input parameters.

The results expose an architecture-dependent limit. In a standard multilayer perceptron, splitting can add detail to a decision boundary, but subsequent learning may move the new nodes back together because the boundaries have long-range effects. The authors report that this problem does not arise for localized receptive-field models such as radial basis functions and Gaussian mixtures, where splitting appears effective.
neurips-1991-node-splitting-a-constructi.tldr: Node splitting expands learned networks where more detail is needed, but works better with localized receptive fields than with standard multilayer perceptrons.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the dependence between separating characters and recognizing them. A character classifier needs an appropriate image region, yet deciding where that region begins and ends can require knowing the character. Touching characters and gaps within a character make a pipeline based on separating images before recognition especially vulnerable.

The proposed COISR approach combines the two decisions in one neural network. In its first version, a backpropagation network scans a field of characters and learns whether its window is centered on one character or lies between characters. When centered on a character, it also identifies that character. Tests on hand-printed digits produce reported very low error rates.

A second version, COISR-SACCADE, additionally learns movements that take the input window from one character to the next. This avoids the exhaustive scanning required by the first version. The shared contribution is to make position and identity decisions cooperate within a learned system, while the second version also incorporates how the system moves through the character field.
neurips-1991-recognizing-overlapping-han.tldr: COISR jointly learns character location and identity, with a second version learning window movements to avoid exhaustive scanning.

paragraphs: This paper applies structural risk minimization to handwritten digit recognition. The central idea is to match a classifier's capacity to the amount of training data available. A model that fits the observed examples well does not necessarily achieve low error on future inputs, so training accuracy alone is an incomplete guide to choosing a classifier.

The authors consider three sources of capacity: properties of the input space, the nature and structure of the classifier, and the learning algorithm. They combine actions across these factors to control the capacity of linear classifiers. This treats generalization as a consequence of the whole learning setup, including how inputs are represented and how the classifier is trained.

The stated result is improved generalization on handwritten digits. The supplied discussion distinguishes minimizing observed training error from minimizing expected error over the full input distribution. Structural risk minimization addresses that distinction by tuning representational capacity to the evidence available. The paper therefore connects a general learning principle to practical choices within a character-recognition system.
neurips-1991-structural-risk-minimizatio.tldr: Coordinating input representation, classifier structure, and learning controls linear-classifier capacity and improves handwritten-digit generalization.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much training data is sufficient for reliable learning in feedforward threshold networks. The networks have multiple outputs, and their weights satisfy specified equivalences. The analysis therefore addresses a model class with both several predicted outputs and structural relationships among its weights, rather than treating all weights as unrestricted.

The authors use the Probably Approximately Correct learning framework. In plain language, this asks how many examples suffice to make a sufficiently accurate learned model likely. They derive an upper bound on that sample requirement with a form similar to the bound for single-output networks without weight equivalences.

The paper reports improvements over the previously available bounds in every case considered. A tighter upper bound gives a stronger sufficient guarantee about the amount of data required; it is a statement about reliable learnability rather than a measured training speed. The result shows that multiple outputs and equivalent weights can be handled within a familiar form of sample-complexity analysis while improving the available guarantees.
neurips-1991-threshold-network-learning-.tldr: PAC analysis improves sample-size upper bounds for multiple-output threshold networks whose weights obey equivalence constraints.
